MPPSC-2023-095.correct_reasoning: 'Mukul' (1930) is a famous collection of Hindi poems by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan; it includes her iconic ballad 'Jhansi Ki Rani' (Khoob ladi mardani, woh toh Jhansi wali rani thi). Hence option D (Subhadra Kumari Chauhan) is correct.
key_concepts: Subhadra Kumari Chauhan (1904-1948): Hindi poetess and freedom fighter; first woman satyagrahi to court arrest in Nagpur (1921); 'Mukul' was her first poetry anthology (November 1930).
Makhanlal Chaturvedi: 'Him Tarangini', 'Him Kiritini'; Bhavani Prasad Mishra: 'Geet Farosh'; Mukutdhar Pandey: nature poetry ('Anshu').
MP literature: Makhanlal Chaturvedi (MP's own, awarded first Sahitya Akademi in Hindi for 'Him Tarangini'); Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's 'Mukul' won her early recognition (Seksaria Prize).
Books-and-authors questions are fixed factual pairs — memorize the mapping.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: 'Mukul' (1930) ➜ Subhadra Kumari Chauhan (contains 'Jhansi Ki Rani').
Chaturvedi = 'Him Tarangini'; Mishra = 'Geet Farosh'.

sources.title: 'Mukul' — poetry collection by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan

MPPSC-2023-096.correct_reasoning: 'Nohdora' (also Naahdora) is the ceremonial clay ornamentation of walls and floors made by the Gond tribe of Madhya Pradesh — painted by both men and women, it is the traditional starting point of Gond wall art (Gond Chinha), now also rendered on paper and canvas. Hence option D (Gond) is correct.
key_concepts: Nohdora: Gond wall/floor ornamentation in clay on mud houses; made on auspicious occasions; Mandla-Dindori-Betul-Balaghat region of MP.
Gond art: one of the largest tribal art traditions; Dravidian Gondi language; Gondwana region.
Other tribes' art: Bhil = Pithora/vibrant dot paintings; Korku and Saharia have their own distinct expressions (not Nohdora).
MP tribes and their art/craft are a repeated MPPSC theme.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Nohdora clay wall ornamentation ➜ Gond tribe.
Bhil = Pithora; Gond = Nohdora/Gond painting.

sources.title: Nohdora — Gond tribe wall ornamentation
sources.citation: MP art and culture / Aadivart Museum

MPPSC-2023-097.correct_reasoning: The Matangeshwar Temple (Matangeshvara Temple), a historic Shiva temple built by the Chandelas, is situated in Khajuraho, Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh. It is part of the Khajuraho Group of Monuments (UNESCO World Heritage Site) and is still an active place of worship. Hence option C (Khajuraho) is correct.
key_concepts: Matangeshwar Temple: Khajuraho (western group); Chandela period (c. 10th-11th century); dedicated to Shiva; one of the few Khajuraho temples still in worship.
Ujjain = Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga; Maheshwar = Ahilyabai Holkar's fort/temples on Narmada; Vidisha = Heliodorus pillar, Udayagiri caves.
Khajuraho temples: built by Chandela rulers (950-1050 CE), famous for Nagara-style architecture and erotic sculptures.
MP heritage sites are a core prelims topic — match temple to city correctly.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Matangeshwar Temple ➜ Khajuraho (Chandela Shiva temple, still worshipped).
Ujjain=Mahakal; Maheshwar=Narmada; Vidisha=Udayagiri.

sources.title: Matangeshwar Temple — Khajuraho

MPPSC-2023-098.correct_reasoning: Ramchandrika is a famous work of Keshavdas (Keshav Das), the 16th-17th century Hindi poet of the Orchha court (Bundelkhand) and founder of the Rasik school of Hindi poetry. His other works include Rasik Priya, Kavipriya, Ratnavati and Jahangir Jas Chandrika. Hence option C (Keshavdas) is correct.
key_concepts: Keshavdas (1555-1617): court poet of Raja Indrajit Singh of Orchha; Rasik school; 'Rasik Priya' (first work, 1591), 'Kavipriya', 'Ratnavati', 'Virsimhadev Charit', 'Jahangir Jas Chandrika', 'Ramchandrika'.
Bhushan: poet of Chhatrasal (Bundela king); 'Shivraj Bhushan'. Padmakar: 'Jagatvilas' etc. Bhavabhuti: Sanskrit playwright (8th century, 'Uttara Ramacharita', 'Malatimadhava').
Bundelkhand (Orchha) literary heritage is MP-specific — Orchha was the seat of Keshavdas.
Ramchandrika = a retelling/poetic work on the Ramayana theme by Keshavdas.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Ramchandrika ➜ Keshavdas (Orchha court poet, Rasik school).
Bhushan = Chhatrasal's poet; Bhavabhuti = Sanskrit.

sources.title: Keshavdas — Ramchandrika, Rasik school
sources.citation: Hindi literature / MP art and culture

MPPSC-2023-099.correct_reasoning: Balkrishna Sharma 'Naveen' (1897-1960), freedom fighter and poet from Shajapur (MP), wrote the two kavyas 'Pranarpan' and 'Atmosarga' on/lamenting Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi, the nationalist journalist and editor of 'Pratap' (Kanpur), who was killed on 25 March 1931 while trying to protect people during the Kanpur communal riots. Naveen succeeded Vidyarthi as editor of Pratap. Hence option A (Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi) is correct. (The question text reads 'Tranarpan/Atmosarga'; the standard titles are 'Pranarpan' and 'Atmosarga'.)
key_concepts: Balkrishna Sharma 'Naveen': born 8 Dec 1897, Shajapur district; editor of Pratap from 1931; nominated to Constituent Assembly; Padma Bhushan (1960); wrote in Khadi Boli, Braj, Awadhi, Bundeli, Urdu, Malwi.
Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi (1890-1931): founder-editor of Hindi newspaper 'Pratap', Kanpur; martyr of communal harmony — killed while rescuing people during Kanpur riots, 25 March 1931.
Pranarpan and Atmosarga are literary tributes to Vidyarthi's sacrifice.
Exam trap: do not confuse Naveen (author) with another poet, or Vidyarthi with another contemporary.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Naveen's 'Pranarpan' & 'Atmosarga' ➜ tribute to Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi (Pratap editor, martyred 1931).
Naveen = Shajapur; Vidyarthi = Pratap, Kanpur.

sources.title: Balkrishna Sharma Naveen — kavyas on Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi

MPPSC-2023-100.correct_reasoning: The Thona-Luhari firing (shootout) incident in Niwari district (Bundelkhand, erstwhile Orchha princely state) took place on 8 February 1939 during the freedom movement, when police opened fire on freedom fighters who had unfurled the national flag at Thona-Luhari village. Hence option C (1939) is correct.
key_concepts: Thona-Luhari (Feb 8, 1939): Bundelkhand State Congress (est. May 1938, led by Lalaram Bajpai and Chaturbhuj Pathak) launched a flag satyagraha against Orchha state rule; police firing killed several freedom fighters.
Documented in the Amrit Mahotsav Digital District Repository (Niwari/Tikamgarh, Bundelkhand).
1942 = Quit India Movement; 1931 = Bhagat Singh etc.; 1922 = Chauri Chaura — all common distractors in freedom-movement chronology.
MP's princely-state praja mandal movements (e.g., against Orchha) are part of the state's freedom struggle narrative.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Thona-Luhari firing ➜ 8 February 1939 (Orchha princely state, Niwari/Bundelkhand).
Chronology trap: 1939 ≠ 1942 (Quit India).

sources.title: Thona-Luhari shootout, 8 February 1939
sources.citation: Amrit Mahotsav Digital District Repository, GoI

MPPSC-2024-001.correct_reasoning: Down syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome 21, i.e. the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21). The condition was first clinically described by John Langdon Down in 1866, and its chromosomal basis was established by Jerome Lejeune in 1959. It is the most common chromosomal disorder in humans and causes characteristic physical features with intellectual disability. Hence option B is correct.
key_concepts: Turner syndrome = monosomy X (45,X), affects females only (missing/partial X chromosome).
Super female syndrome = trisomy X (47,XXX), an extra X chromosome in females.
Klinefelter syndrome = 47,XXY, an extra X chromosome in males.
None of Turner, Super Female or Klinefelter involves chromosome 21; all are sex-chromosome aneuploidies.
Down syndrome risk rises with maternal age; incidence roughly 1 in 700–1,000 live births.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Trisomy 21 = Down syndrome. Think chromosome '21' ➜ 'Down'.
All other options are sex-chromosome (X/Y) disorders, not chromosome-21 disorders.

sources.title: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Principles of Inheritance and Variation (chromosomal disorders)
MedlinePlus Genetics – Down Syndrome (trisomy 21)

MPPSC-2024-002.correct_reasoning: The National Health Policy (NHP) 2017 aims at universal health coverage and calls for coordinated action in seven priority areas to improve the health environment: (1) Swachh Bharat Abhiyan; (2) balanced, healthy diets and regular exercise; (3) addressing tobacco, alcohol and substance abuse; (4) Yatri Suraksha — preventing deaths due to rail and road traffic accidents; (5) Nirbhaya Nari — action against gender violence; (6) reduced stress and improved safety at the workplace; (7) reducing indoor and outdoor air pollution. The Annapurna Scheme (food security for eligible senior citizens not covered by an old-age pension) is a social-welfare/food-security scheme and is NOT one of these seven health priority areas. Hence option D is correct.
key_concepts: NHP 2017 succeeded the National Health Policies of 1983 and 2002.
Aspirational goal: raise government health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025.
Annapurna Scheme was launched on 1 April 2000 to provide food security to senior citizens eligible for but not receiving an old-age pension.
The seven NHP 2017 areas are coordinated cross-sectoral actions, not a list of all health schemes.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Annapurna = food for the aged (welfare), whereas NHP 2017's seven areas are health-environment actions — Annapurna does not belong.
The odd one out is Annapurna Scheme (D).

sources.title: National Health Policy 2017, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

MPPSC-2024-003.correct_reasoning: Lathyrism is a neuroparalytic disorder (spastic paraparesis of the lower limbs) caused by chronic excessive consumption of khesari dal (grass pea, Lathyrus sativus). Khesari dal contains the neurotoxic amino acid beta-N-oxalylamino-L-alanine (BOAA, also called ODAP). Prolonged consumption damages upper motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness and paralysis of the legs. Hence option A is correct.
key_concepts: Chana dal (chickpea) and moong dal (green gram) do not contain BOAA and do not cause lathyrism.
The Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) has developed low-BOAA khesari strains through tissue-culture/breeding work.
Lathyrism is prevalent where khesari dal is a dietary staple — parts of Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Bangladesh and Ethiopia.
MP connection: 'lokhand' (lathyrism) is a recognized public-health concern in khesari-consuming belts of Madhya Pradesh.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Khesari dal ➜ BOAA toxin ➜ Lathyrism (leg paralysis).
Think 'K' for Khesari and 'L' for Lathyrism.

sources.title: National Institute of Nutrition / ICMR — Khesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) and BOAA neurolathyrism

MPPSC-2024-004.correct_reasoning: On 15 February 2017, ISRO's Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle PSLV-C37 successfully launched 104 satellites in a single flight from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota — a world record for the most satellites launched by one rocket at that time. The primary payload was Cartosat-2 Series, accompanied by 103 nano/international satellites. Hence option D is correct.
key_concepts: PSLV is ISRO's workhorse launch vehicle, mainly used for polar/sun-synchronous orbits and small satellites.
INSAT-3DR is an advanced meteorological/communication satellite, not a 104-satellite mission.
PSLV-C55 (2023) and GSLV-F12 (2023) are different, later missions.
Most of the 104 co-passengers on PSLV-C37 were foreign (mainly US) nano-satellites; the flight underlined ISRO's commercial launch capability.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: 15 Feb 2017 ➜ PSLV-C37 ➜ 104 satellites (world record then).
C37 = Cartosat-2 series primary payload; the number 104 is the key exam fact.

sources.title: ISRO — PSLV-C37 / Cartosat-2 Series Mission, 15 February 2017

MPPSC-2024-005.correct_reasoning: The thickness (total column amount) of the ozone layer is measured in Dobson Units (DU), named after G. M. B. Dobson. One DU corresponds to a layer of pure ozone 0.01 mm thick at standard temperature and pressure. Normal values are around 300 DU; readings below about 220 DU define an 'ozone hole'. Hence option B is correct.
key_concepts: Decibels measure sound intensity, not ozone.
PPB (parts per billion) and PPM (parts per million) express gas concentrations, not total column ozone thickness.
Ozone is measured with Dobson spectrophotometers and by satellite instruments such as TOMS/OMI.
The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C radiation; the Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Ozone thickness ➜ Dobson Units (DU). Think 'D' for Dobson and 'Ozone'.
Do not confuse DU (total column ozone) with PPB/PPM (trace-gas concentration).

sources.title: NASA Ozone Watch — Dobson Unit

MPPSC-2024-006.correct_reasoning: A human vertebral column has 7 cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) in the neck region. This number is remarkably constant across mammals — even a giraffe has only 7 cervical vertebrae. C1 is the atlas and C2 is the axis. Hence option B is correct.
key_concepts: The adult vertebral column has 33 vertebrae in all: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral (fused into sacrum) and 4 coccygeal (fused into coccyx).
Option D's '33' is the total number of vertebrae, not the cervical count (and the trailing '2' appears to be a printing artifact).
Cervical vertebrae are the smallest and most mobile vertebrae and support the skull.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: 7 cervical vertebrae — '7 in the neck' (C1 atlas, C2 axis).
Recall the full count as 7-12-5-5-4 (cervical-thoracic-lumbar-sacral-coccygeal).

sources.title: NCERT Class 11 Biology, Locomotion and Movement (vertebral column)

MPPSC-2024-007.correct_reasoning: India's first interplanetary mission was the Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), also called Mangalyaan. It was launched on 5 November 2013 aboard PSLV-C25 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, and entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014. Hence option A (2013) is correct.
key_concepts: MOM made ISRO the fourth space agency to reach Mars orbit and the first Asian nation to do so.
India succeeded in its very first attempt to Mars, and the mission was notably cost-effective (around ₹450 crore).
The launch vehicle was PSLV-C25 (not GSLV), because MOM was a relatively light spacecraft.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: MOM/Mangalyaan launched 5 November 2013 (PSLV-C25); Mars orbit reached 24 September 2014.
First interplanetary = Mars; year = 2013.

sources.title: ISRO — Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM / Mangalyaan)

MPPSC-2024-008.correct_reasoning: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted by Parliament in 1974. It was India's first major environmental legislation, aimed at preventing and controlling water pollution and maintaining/restoring the wholesomeness of water. It also led to the constitution of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs). Hence option D (1974) is correct.
key_concepts: 1972 is associated with the UN Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment, not the Water Act.
The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act came in 1981; the Environment (Protection) Act came in 1986 (after the Bhopal gas tragedy).
CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water Act.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Water Act = 1974 — India's first major environmental law; it created CPCB and SPCBs.
Sequence: Water Act 1974 → Air Act 1981 → Environment Protection Act 1986.

sources.title: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 — Central Pollution Control Board

MPPSC-2024-009.correct_reasoning: Under the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by the UN in 2015: SDG 1 = No Poverty; SDG 2 = Zero Hunger; SDG 9 = Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure. Hence option A is correct.

option_explanations.text: No poverty; Zero hunger; Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure
No poverty; Quality education; Life on land
Clean water and sanitation; Climate action; Sustainable cities and communities
Gender equality; Climate action; Zero hunger

key_concepts: SDG 4 = Quality Education; SDG 5 = Gender Equality; SDG 6 = Clean Water and Sanitation; SDG 13 = Climate Action; SDG 11 = Sustainable Cities and Communities; SDG 15 = Life on Land.
There are 17 SDGs and 169 targets, with a target year of 2030.
India tracks SDG progress through the NITI Aayog SDG India Index.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: SDG 1–2–9 = No Poverty – Zero Hunger – Industry/Innovation/Infrastructure.
Match each SDG number to its title; option A is the only one with all three correct.

sources.title: United Nations — Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
NITI Aayog — SDG India Index

MPPSC-2024-010.correct_reasoning: In a pond (aquatic) ecosystem, fungi and bacteria act as decomposers (saprotrophs). They secrete enzymes onto dead organic matter (dead plants and animals), break it down into simpler inorganic substances, and release the nutrients back into the soil/water for reuse by producers. Hence option C is correct.
key_concepts: Autotrophs (producers) = green plants and algae that make their own food by photosynthesis.
Consumers = herbivores, carnivores and omnivores that eat other organisms.
Abiotic components = non-living factors such as light, temperature, water and dissolved nutrients.
Decomposers complete nutrient cycling in an ecosystem.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Fungi and bacteria = nature's recyclers = decomposers (saprotrophs).
Dead matter ➜ fungi/bacteria ➜ nutrients returned to producers.

sources.title: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ecosystem (ecosystem components: producers, consumers, decomposers)

MPPSC-2024-011.correct_reasoning: In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Supreme Court of India held that Fundamental Rights would prevail over the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in the event of a conflict, because Fundamental Rights are justiciable/enforceable by courts while DPSPs are non-justiciable. This conflict and its resolution directly led to the First Constitutional Amendment (1951). Hence option B is correct.

option_explanations.text: The State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
Kesavananda Bharati v. the State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. the Union of India (1980)

key_concepts: Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot curtail Fundamental Rights.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): introduced the 'basic structure' doctrine.
Minerva Mills (1980): restored balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs; declared judicial review part of basic structure.
The 1951 Champakam judgment prompted the First Amendment (Articles 15(4), 31A/31B and the Ninth Schedule).
FR vs DPSP hierarchy: FRs are enforceable; DPSPs are directive but not enforceable by courts.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) ➜ Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSP ➜ led to First Amendment (1951).
It is the earliest of the four cases listed and the one that resolved FR-vs-DPSP precedence first.

sources.title: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) — Supreme Court of India

MPPSC-2024-012.correct_reasoning: The question asks which statement about the Election Commission of India is NOT correct. Option A is incorrect: differences of opinion among the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners are decided by the Election Commission itself (by majority), not by the Law Commission. Since A is the false statement, it is the answer to a 'not correct' question. Hence option A is correct.

option_explanations.text: In case of differences of opinion amongst the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, the matter is decided by the Law Commission.
The Election Commissioners cannot be removed from their office except on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
The Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners enjoy equal powers.
The term of office of Election Commissioners is six years from the date they assume office or till the day they attain the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.

key_concepts: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission.
CEC and other ECs have equal powers; decisions are by majority.
CEC can be removed like a Supreme Court judge; other ECs can be removed only on the CEC's recommendation (Article 324(5)).
Term: six years or age 65, whichever is earlier. The Law Commission is a legal-reform body, not an electoral-dispute authority.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: EC differences decided by the Commission (majority), NOT the Law Commission — so A is the 'not correct' statement.
For 'not correct' questions, pick the statement that is factually false.

sources.title: Article 324 and the Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991

MPPSC-2024-013.correct_reasoning: Under the proviso to Article 368(2), certain constitutional amendments require, in addition to a special majority in Parliament, ratification by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States. Article 279A (which constitutes the GST Council) was added to this mandatory-ratification list by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, so any change to Article 279A needs both a special majority and ratification by at least half the state legislatures. Hence option D is correct.

option_explanations.text: If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 53.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 239A.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 243A.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 279A.

key_concepts: Other ratification-triggering provisions: election of the President (Arts 54, 55), extent of executive power (Arts 73, 74), judiciary (Arts 124–147, 214–231), High Courts for states, the Seventh Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself.
Articles 53 (Union executive power), 239A and 243A (local bodies) are not in this mandatory half-state ratification list.
Half of the states means roughly 14–15 state legislatures must pass resolutions ratifying the amendment before the President's assent.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Article 279A (GST Council) — changes need special majority + ratification by half the state legislatures (101st Amendment, 2016).
Ratification = federal feature protecting state interests.

sources.title: Article 368, Constitution of India; 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 (GST)

MPPSC-2024-014.correct_reasoning: Article 61 of the Constitution lays down the procedure for the impeachment of the President of India for 'violation of the Constitution'. The charge may be preferred in either House of Parliament, requires signatures of one-fourth of its members, must be passed by a two-thirds majority of the total membership of that House, is then investigated by the other House, and if sustained by a two-thirds majority, results in the President's removal. Hence option C (Article 61) is correct.
key_concepts: Article 60 = President's oath/affirmation; Article 62 = time of election to fill vacancy and term; Article 63 = Vice-President of India.
Impeachment is a quasi-judicial, parliamentary process; the only ground is 'violation of the Constitution'.
No President of India has ever been impeached.
The nominated members of Parliament also take part in the impeachment process.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Impeachment of the President ➜ Article 61.
Articles 60 (oath), 62 (vacancy), 63 (Vice-President) are the nearby distractors.

sources.title: Article 61, Constitution of India (Procedure for impeachment of the President)

MPPSC-2024-015.correct_reasoning: Article 76 of the Constitution provides for the Attorney General for India, who is appointed by the President and must be a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court (i.e., a citizen of India who has been a judge of a High Court for at least five years, or an advocate of a High Court/Supreme Court for at least ten years, or is in the President's opinion an eminent jurist). Hence option C is correct.

option_explanations.text: who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the High Court.
who has been an advocate of the Supreme Court for at least seven years.
who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court.
who has been an advocate of the High Court for at least seven years.

key_concepts: The Attorney General is the highest law officer of India and advises the Government of India on legal matters.
He/She has the right of audience in all courts in India and can participate in Parliament proceedings but cannot vote.
The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President and is not a member of the Cabinet (unlike in some other systems).
Qualification threshold is Supreme Court-judge level, not High Court-judge level.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Attorney General (Article 76) ➜ qualified to be a Supreme Court Judge.
AG = highest law officer; SC-judge qualification; right of audience in all courts.

sources.title: Article 76, Constitution of India (Attorney General for India)

MPPSC-2024-016.correct_reasoning: K. M. Munshi (Kanhaiyalal Maneklal Munshi) was a member of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, which was chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. He was also a freedom fighter, lawyer and the founder of Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan. Hence option B (Constitution Draft Committee) is correct.
key_concepts: The Drafting Committee had seven members: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar (chairman), K. M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Iyer, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Syed Mohammad Saadulla, B. L. Mitter and D. P. Khaitan.
The Public Accounts Committee is a parliamentary financial committee (not a Constituent Assembly body).
The Preamble was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru (Objectives Resolution, 1946); there was no separate 'Preamble Committee' headed by Munshi.
The Hindu Code Bill was associated mainly with Dr. Ambedkar as Law Minister, not with Munshi's Constituent Assembly role.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: K. M. Munshi ➜ member of the Drafting Committee (chaired by Dr. Ambedkar).
Drafting Committee = 7 members; Munshi was one of them.

sources.title: Constituent Assembly of India — Drafting Committee members
sources.citation: Constitution of India / Parliament of India

MPPSC-2024-017.correct_reasoning: Under Article 352 of the Constitution, the President may proclaim a National Emergency only on the written advice of the Union Cabinet (the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 made the Cabinet's written advice mandatory, so the President cannot act on the Prime Minister's advice alone). Hence option C (Union Cabinet) is correct.
key_concepts: Article 352 grounds: war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month (by special majority) and remains in force for six months, extendable.
'Council of Ministers' is broader than the 'Union Cabinet'; the Constitution specifically requires the Cabinet's written advice for an emergency proclamation.
The 44th Amendment (1978) also replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' to prevent misuse.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: National Emergency (Article 352) ➜ President acts on the Union Cabinet's written advice (44th Amendment).
Not the PM alone — it is the Cabinet.

sources.title: Article 352, Constitution of India (Proclamation of Emergency); 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978

MPPSC-2024-018.correct_reasoning: The Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Good Governance and Policy Analysis (AIGGPA), formerly the School of Good Governance and Policy Analysis, is located in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. It was set up by the Madhya Pradesh Government in September 2007 and functions at Sushasan Bhawan, Bhopal. Hence option C (Bhopal) is correct; the earlier key of New Delhi was factually wrong and contradicted the question's own explanation.

option_explanations.reason: New Delhi hosts other policy institutes, but not this one.
Hyderabad is not the seat of this institute.
Correct. The Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Good Governance and Policy Analysis is located in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
Jabalpur is not the seat of this institute.

key_concepts: AIGGPA is an autonomous think-tank of the Government of Madhya Pradesh for policy analysis, governance research and training (e-governance, citizen-centric services).
It is distinct from national institutions located in Delhi such as the Lokpal or IIPA.
MP connection: it supports the MP state government in formulating and implementing policy frameworks.
The institute's address is Sushasan Bhawan, Bhadbhada Chouraha, Bhopal.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: AIGGPA (good governance institute) ➜ Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
Answer key correction: New Delhi (A) was wrong; correct answer is Bhopal (C).

sources.title: Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Good Governance and Policy Analysis (AIGGPA), Bhopal

MPPSC-2024-020.correct_reasoning: The Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution, added by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992), lists 29 functions/matters (e.g., agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, animal husbandry, primary education, health and sanitation) that may be entrusted to Panchayats (rural local bodies) by state legislatures. Hence option A (Eleventh Schedule) is correct.
key_concepts: Twelfth Schedule (74th Amendment, 1992) lists 18 functions for Municipalities (urban local bodies) — not Panchayats.

MPPSC-2024-031.correct_reasoning: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is the percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that banks must maintain in liquid assets (cash, gold, approved securities). Until 2007, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 prescribed a lower ceiling (floor) of 25% for SLR. The 2007 amendment removed this 25% lower ceiling, giving the RBI flexibility to prescribe SLR within a band. Hence option B (25%) is correct.
key_concepts: SLR is a monetary-tool reserve; CRR is the cash portion kept with RBI (no interest), while SLR assets earn some return.
After 2007, RBI sets SLR; current SLR is 18% (as of recent policy), showing the downward flexibility gained after the floor was removed.
The 25% figure is the statutory lower ceiling that existed before 2007 — the precise fact being tested.
MPPSC economy questions often test statutory floors/ceilings removed or retained by amendments.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: SLR lower ceiling before 2007 = 25%; removed by Banking Regulation Act amendment 2007.
SLR vs CRR: SLR = liquid assets with the bank itself; CRR = cash with RBI.

MPPSC-2024-032.correct_reasoning: India's external debt to GDP ratio stood at about 18.6% at the end of September 2023, according to RBI/Department of Economic Affairs external debt statistics. External debt is the total debt a country owes to foreign (non-resident) creditors; expressing it as a share of GDP indicates repayment capacity and vulnerability. India's ratio is considered low and prudent, with adequate foreign-exchange reserves covering external debt. Hence option A (18.6%) is correct.
key_concepts: External debt = sovereign + private debt owed to non-residents (World Bank, IMF, foreign borrowings, NRI deposits, trade credit, etc.).
DEA (Ministry of Finance) and RBI publish India's external debt quarterly; end-September 2023 figure ≈ 18.6% of GDP.
A low external-debt-to-GDP ratio (under ~20%) signals manageable external liabilities; India's forex reserves provide additional cover.
Do not confuse with domestic fiscal deficit or central-government debt/GDP.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: India's external debt/GDP, end-Sept 2023 ≈ 18.6% (RBI/DEA).
Low + forex-reserve-covered ➜ India's external position is comfortable.

sources.title: Reserve Bank of India / Department of Economic Affairs — India's External Debt statistics

MPPSC-2024-041.correct_reasoning: The kernel is the core (central) part of the UNIX operating system. MPPSC-2024-042.correct_reasoning: A phishing attack comes in the form of deceptive emails or text messages that appear to come from a legitimate source and ask the user to install software, click a malicious link, or reveal credentials/personal information. Hence option C (Phishing) is correct.

MPPSC-2024-044.correct_reasoning: 'The Imitation Game' was the original name Alan Turing gave, in his 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', to what is now known as the Turing Test — a test of whether a machine can exhibit intelligent behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human. 'All of the above' is wrong because only the Turing Test matches.

Its role is to make sure the Web works consistently across browsers and devices (interoperability).
Tim Berners-Lee, inventor of the World Wide Web, is its director.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: W3C = World Wide Web Consortium (web standards body).
Consortium sets open web standards such as HTML and CSS.

sources.title: World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)

MPPSC-2024-051.correct_reasoning: In Madhya Pradesh, wheat ranks first among cereals in terms of both area sown and production. Wheat is the major food crop of the state (MP is among the top wheat-producing states in India, e.g., over 22 million tonnes in 2021–22), with Hoshangabad a leading district. Hence option D (First) is correct.
key_concepts: Among food grains/cereals in MP, wheat is the most important crop by area and production (rice and maize follow).
MP is often called a major contributor to India's wheat pool (second only to Punjab in some years).
The question asks for the position among cereals in MP — wheat is first.
Hoshangabad (Narmadapuram) district leads in wheat area and production within MP.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Wheat ➜ first among cereals in Madhya Pradesh (area and production).
MP is a leading wheat state nationally too.

MPPSC-2024-052.correct_reasoning: Soybean farming in Madhya Pradesh was initially started in Dewas district (as a pilot project). MP is the largest producer of soybeans in India and is called the 'Soyabean Capital of India', though Ujjain is now the highest-producing district within the state. Hence option D (Dewas) is correct.
key_concepts: Ujjain is the highest soybean-producing district in MP — a common distractor; but the question asks where soybean farming was *initially started*, which is Dewas.
MP's Malwa region (black soil) is ideal for soybean; excluding Singrauli, most MP districts grow soybean.
Soybean is a kharif crop and a major oilseed of MP.
Do not confuse 'highest producer now' (Ujjain) with 'where it was started' (Dewas).
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Soybean farming started in Dewas (MP); Ujjain produces the most now.
Started = Dewas; highest producer = Ujjain — keep them distinct.

MPPSC-2024-053.correct_reasoning: Rock phosphate is used primarily in the fertilizer industry, where it is processed into phosphate fertilizers that supply phosphorus, a key plant nutrient. Hence option B (Fertilizer industry) is correct.
key_concepts: Rock phosphate is the principal raw material for phosphatic fertilisers (e.g., single super phosphate, DAP).
Textile, sugar and paper industries do not use rock phosphate as a key input.
MP has rock-phosphate deposits and is a significant fertiliser-consuming state (agrarian economy).
Phosphorus (P) is one of the three primary plant nutrients (N-P-K).
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Rock phosphate ➜ fertilizer industry (phosphorus for crops).
Rock phosphate = raw material for phosphate fertilisers.

MPPSC-2024-054.correct_reasoning: Rainfall in Madhya Pradesh decreases from east to west and south to north. The southeastern part of MP receives the maximum rainfall from the Bay of Bengal branch of the southwest monsoon. Hence option B (Bay of Bengal branch of monsoon) is correct.

option_explanations.text: Bay of Bengal branch of monsoon

key_concepts: The Arabian Sea branch mainly affects western MP; the Bay of Bengal branch brings moisture to eastern and southeastern MP.
Eastern/southeastern MP districts (e.g., Balaghat, Mandla, Seoni, Shahdol) receive higher rainfall than western MP.
Retreating monsoon and cyclones contribute relatively little to MP's annual rainfall.
MP's average rainfall is around 1,100–1,200 mm, unevenly distributed.

Rainfall in MP decreases from east to west.

MPPSC-2024-055.correct_reasoning: Black soil (regur) in Madhya Pradesh is formed by the weathering of basaltic lava rocks of the Deccan Trap. It is rich in iron, lime, calcium, aluminium and magnesia, retains moisture, and is well known for cotton cultivation. Hence option C (Basalt) is correct.
key_concepts: Sandstone, limestone and gneiss weather into other soil types, not the characteristic black regur soil of MP.
Black soil is found extensively in the Narmada valley and Malwa Plateau of MP.
It is self-ploughing (develops cracks when dry), holds moisture well, and suits cotton.
MP's black soil derives from the volcanic Deccan Traps that cover much of western/central India.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Black soil (regur) of MP ➜ weathered basalt (Deccan Trap).
Black soil = cotton soil = basalt origin.

sources.title: Soils of Madhya Pradesh — black soil from Deccan Trap basalt

MPPSC-2024-056.correct_reasoning: Bamboo was nationalised in Madhya Pradesh in 1973, bringing the management of bamboo forests under the state government's control to regulate collection, processing and marketing, and to prevent exploitation of forest dwellers by intermediaries. Hence option C (1973) is correct.
key_concepts: MP was the first state to nationalise a forest produce; bamboo (a grass, botanically Bambusoideae) was nationalised in 1973.
Major forest produce in MP includes teak, sal and bamboo; minor forest produce includes tendu leaf, gum, harra, amla, mahua.
Nationalisation aimed at fair prices for forest dwellers and state control over industrial use (paper, baskets, construction).
MP stands second in bamboo production after Arunachal Pradesh.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Bamboo nationalised in Madhya Pradesh ➜ 1973.
MP was first state to nationalise a forest produce (bamboo, 1973).

sources.title: Forests of Madhya Pradesh — nationalisation of bamboo, 1973

MPPSC-2024-057.correct_reasoning: The Bhander Plateau is considered the southern part of the Vindhyan Plateau (Vindhyan scarpland) in Madhya Pradesh. Hence option C (Bhander plateau) is correct.
key_concepts: Amarkantak plateau (Maikal range) is the source of the Narmada and Son rivers; Maikal plateau lies in eastern MP; Bastar plateau is in Chhattisgarh.
The Vindhyan range runs across MP; its southern portion in MP is identified with the Bhander Plateau.
Bhander Plateau is located in the southern part of the Vindhyan region of MP.
Physiography of MP (Malwa, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand, Mahakoshal, Vindhyan, Satpura) is a recurring MPPSC geography theme.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Southern part of Vindhyan scarpland ➜ Bhander Plateau.
Amarkantak = Narmada source; Bastar = Chhattisgarh (not MP).

sources.title: Physiography of Madhya Pradesh — plateaus (MP geography)

MPPSC-2024-058.correct_reasoning: The Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) plant at Bhopal was established with technical collaboration/support from a company of Britain — Associated Electrical Industries (AEI) of the UK. Heavy Electricals (India) Ltd was set up at Bhopal in 1956 with British collaboration to manufacture turbines, generators, transformers and switchgear. Hence option D (Britain) is correct.
key_concepts: The Bhopal unit's initial collaboration was British (AEI UK); other BHEL plants later used Russian (Hardwar) and Czechoslovak (Hyderabad, Tiruchirapalli) collaboration — hence Germany/France/Russia are distractors.
BHEL was formed as a separate company in 1962 and merged with HEIL later.
BHEL is India's largest engineering and manufacturing enterprise for power equipment.
The Bhopal plant was the first heavy electrical plant in India.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: BHEL Bhopal ➜ British collaboration (AEI UK).
Bhopal = Britain; Hardwar = Russia; Hyderabad/Tiruchirapalli = Czechoslovakia.

sources.title: BHEL Bhopal — established in technical collaboration with AEI UK

MPPSC-2024-059.correct_reasoning: According to the 2011 Census, Bhopal district had the highest percentage of urban population among the listed MP districts (about 80.9% urban). Indore is the most populous district, but Bhopal has the highest urban share. Hence option C (Bhopal) is correct.
key_concepts: Indore is MP's most populous district (2011), but not the most urbanised by percentage.
Dindori had the minimum urban population percentage (around 4.6%); MP as a whole was about 27.6% urban in 2011.
Urban population = people living in urban areas (towns/cities) as defined by the Census.
State capital Bhopal is highly urbanised relative to other MP districts.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Highest urban population % in MP (2011) ➜ Bhopal (~80.9%).
Most populous (Indore) ≠ most urbanised (Bhopal) — keep distinct.

sources.title: Census of India 2011 — Madhya Pradesh district urban population

MPPSC-2024-060.correct_reasoning: The Sardar Sarovar Project (on the Narmada River) is a multipurpose project involving a partnership of four states: Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan, as allocated by the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal. Hence option D (Sardar Sarovar Project) is correct.
key_concepts: Bansagar (Son River) involves MP, UP and Bihar — three states, not four.
Rajghat (Betwa River) is an MP–Uttar Pradesh project — two states.
Sardar Sarovar is a major multipurpose dam (irrigation, hydropower, drinking water) benefiting Gujarat most, with water shared among the four basin states.
The question asks for the project where *four states* have a partnership — Sardar Sarovar.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Sardar Sarovar (Narmada) ➜ 4 states — Gujarat, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan.
Bansagar = 3 states (MP, UP, Bihar); Rajghat = 2 states (MP, UP).

sources.title: Sardar Sarovar Project / Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal award — four basin states

MPPSC-2024-061.correct_reasoning: Durgesh Nandini (Durgeshnandini) is a historical romance novel written in Bengali by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (Bankim Chandra Chatterjee), published in 1865. It was Bankim Chandra's first Bengali novel and one of the earliest modern Indian novels. Hence option B (Bankim Chandra Chatterjee) is correct.
key_concepts: Rabindranath Tagore wrote Gitanjali, Gora, etc.; Hemchandra Bandopadhyay wrote 'Bharat Vidhata' (the line 'Jana Gana Mana' echo) — neither wrote Durgeshnandini.
Bankim Chandra also wrote Anandamath (source of 'Vande Mataram') and Kapalkundala.
Durgeshnandini marked the beginning of the Bengali novel and Indian fiction in English translation influence.
Bankim Chandra Chatterjee (1838–1894) is regarded as a father of the modern Indian novel.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Durgesh Nandini ➜ Bankim Chandra Chatterjee (1865), first Bengali novel.
Bankim Chandra = Vande Mataram (Anandamath) and Durgeshnandini.

sources.title: Durgeshnandini by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (1865)

MPPSC-2024-062.correct_reasoning: Keshav Chandra Sen was appointed Chief Acharya of the Brahmo Samaj by Debendranath Tagore (also written Devendranath Thakur), who had joined the Brahmo Samaj in 1842 and was its leader. Later, Keshav Chandra Sen broke away and formed the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866). Hence option C (Devendranath Thakur) is correct.
key_concepts: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828); Debendranath Tagore succeeded him and led the Tattwabodhini/Brahmo tradition.
Keshav Chandra Sen was a prominent Brahmo leader who later split (Brahmo Samaj of India, 1866) and emphasized Christian-like devotion.
N. G. Chandavarkar and M. G. Ranade were associated with the Prarthana Samaj and social reform in western India.
Brahmo Samaj opposed idol worship, caste and sati; promoted monotheism and modern education.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Keshav Chandra Sen made Chief Acharya by Debendranath Thakur (Brahmo Samaj).
Ram Mohan Roy founded Brahmo Samaj; Debendranath led it; Keshav Chandra Sen later split.

sources.title: Brahmo Samaj — Ram Mohan Roy, Debendranath Tagore, Keshav Chandra Sen

MPPSC-2024-063.correct_reasoning: Mahatma Gandhi called for a boycott of the Prince of Wales (later Edward VIII) during his visit to India in 1921, as part of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22). The boycott was part of the wider programme of surrendering titles, boycotting courts, schools and foreign goods. Hence option B (Non-Cooperation Movement) is correct.
key_concepts: Khilafat Movement (1919–24) was about the Ottoman Caliph and was merged with Non-Cooperation by Gandhi, but the Prince of Wales boycott belongs to Non-Cooperation.
Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Dandi March (1930); Quit India in 1942 ('Do or Die').
The Non-Cooperation Movement was suspended after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922).
The Prince of Wales visit (Nov 1921) was greeted with hartals and boycotts.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Boycott of Prince of Wales (1921) ➜ Non-Cooperation Movement.
Non-Cooperation (1920-22) → Civil Disobedience (1930) → Quit India (1942) in sequence.

sources.title: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22), Indian National Movement

MPPSC-2024-064.correct_reasoning: In the Mauryan administrative system, the Pradeshta was connected with the judiciary/justice department. The Pradeshika was the district administrator, while the Pradeshta functioned in the judicial sphere. Hence option B (Justice Department) is correct.
key_concepts: Mauryan administration (from Kautilya's Arthashastra and Megasthenes): the empire was divided into provinces, districts and villages; officials included Pradeshika (district head), Yukta, and Pradeshta (judicial).
Revenue was handled by officials such as the Samaharta (collector-general) and Sannidhata (treasurer).
Military was under the Senapati and a war board with six sub-committees (per Megasthenes).
The Pradeshta's judicial role distinguishes it from the revenue and military arms.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Mauryan Pradeshta ➜ Justice (judicial) department.
Pradeshika = district administrator; Pradeshta = judicial — similar names, different roles.

sources.title: Mauryan administration — Arthashastra of Kautilya and Megasthenes' Indica

MPPSC-2024-065.correct_reasoning: K. M. Panikkar (K. M. Pannikar), the historian and diplomat, described Gopal Krishna Gokhale as 'the first diplomat of modern India' for his measured, constitutional approach and his role in presenting India's case to the British. Hence option C (Gopal Krishna Gokhale) is correct.
key_concepts: Gokhale was a moderate leader, mentor of Gandhi, founder of the Servants of India Society (1905), and advocated constitutional methods and social reform.
Dadabhai Naoroji = 'Grand Old Man of India', first to demand Swaraj (1906 Calcutta session), drain-of-wealth theory.
Tilak = extremist, 'Swaraj is my birthright'; Lajpat Rai = Punjab nationalist ('Lal Bal Pal').
Panikkar's phrase highlights Gokhale's diplomatic, persuasive engagement with the colonial power.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: 'First diplomat of modern India' (K. M. Panikkar) ➜ Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
Gokhale = moderate, Servants of India Society, Gandhi's political guru.

sources.title: K. M. Panikkar on Gopal Krishna Gokhale — modern Indian history reference

MPPSC-2024-066.correct_reasoning: The Atharvaveda mentions the Sabha and Samiti as two distinct institutions and refers to them as the 'daughters of Prajapati' (the creator), reflecting their importance in Vedic polity as assemblies. Hence option C (Atharvaveda) is correct.
key_concepts: Sabha and Samiti were Vedic popular assemblies (Sabha = council of elders/nobles; Samiti = broader assembly of the people) involved in governance and electing chiefs.
The Rigveda also mentions them but the Atharvaveda explicitly treats them as two separate institutions/daughters of Prajapati — the standard textbook answer for this phrasing.
Later, with the rise of kingship, these assemblies lost prominence.
This is a standard ancient-history fact tested in MPSC/UPSC-style prelims.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Sabha and Samiti as two separate institutions ➜ Atharvaveda ('daughters of Prajapati').
Vedic assemblies: Sabha (council) and Samiti (people's assembly).

sources.title: Atharvaveda — Sabha and Samiti as daughters of Prajapati

MPPSC-2024-067.correct_reasoning: In the Upanayana (sacred-thread) ritual of the Kshatriya varna, the prescribed mantra was the Trishtubh Mantra. (By contrast, the Brahmin boy recited the Gayatri Mantra and the Vaishya the Jagati Mantra, in the traditional scheme.) Hence option D (Trishtubh Mantra) is correct.
key_concepts: Traditional varna-wise Upanayana mantras: Brahmin — Gayatri; Kshatriya — Trishtubh; Vaishya — Jagati.
Gayatri Mantra is the best-known and is associated with Brahmins — a common distractor here.
Upanayana marked the initiation ('second birth') of the twice-born varnas (dvija).
Trishtubh is a Vedic metre; the association of specific metres with varnas is a ritual-detail fact.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Kshatriya Upanayana mantra ➜ Trishtubh Mantra.
Brahmin=Gayatri, Kshatriya=Trishtubh, Vaishya=Jagati.

sources.title: Vedic Upanayana ritual and varna-wise mantras

MPPSC-2024-068.correct_reasoning: The most famous Kailash temple (Kailasanatha) among the cave temples is located at the Ellora caves in Maharashtra. It is a rock-cut, monolithic temple attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century CE) and is the largest monolithic rock excavation in the world. Hence option B (caves of Ellora) is correct.
key_concepts: Ajanta caves are Buddhist (mainly viharas and chaityas, 2nd century BCE–5th century CE).
Elephanta caves are known for the Shiva Trimurti; Kanheri for Buddhist caves near Mumbai.
Ellora (c. 6th–10th century CE) has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves; Cave 16 is the Kailash temple.
The Kailash temple was carved out of a single basalt rock (top-down excavation).
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Kailash temple ➜ Ellora caves (Cave 16), Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.
Ajanta = Buddhist; Ellora = Kailash (Hindu); Elephanta = Shiva Trimurti.

sources.title: Kailasa temple, Ellora — UNESCO World Heritage Site

MPPSC-2024-069.correct_reasoning: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas and is considered the earliest composition in the history of Indian literature/religion. It consists of 1,028 hymns (suktas) arranged in 10 mandalas, composed in early Vedic Sanskrit. Hence option A (Rigveda) is correct.
key_concepts: The four Vedas in order: Rigveda (oldest), Samaveda (melodies/chants), Yajurveda (ritual formulas), Atharvaveda (spells, charms, everyday concerns).
Rigveda is divided into 10 mandalas; famous hymns include the Purusha Sukta and Nasadiya Sukta.
The Rigvedic period is called the Early Vedic period (c. 1500–1000 BCE).
This is one of the most standard ancient-history facts: Rigveda is the earliest Veda.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Earliest Veda ➜ Rigveda.
Rigveda = oldest Veda; 10 mandalas; Early Vedic period.

sources.title: The Rigveda — oldest of the four Vedas

MPPSC-2024-070.correct_reasoning: Under Ashtanga (eight-limbed) Yoga, the Antaranga (internal) sadhana comprises the inner limbs — principally Dharana (concentration, 6th limb), Dhyana (meditation, 7th) and Samadhi (8th), with Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses, 5th) sometimes treated as the bridge. Among the options, Dharana (rendered 'Dharna' in the paper) is the representative Antaranga sadhana. Hence option D is correct.
key_concepts: Ashtanga Yoga (Patanjali): Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama (first four = Bahiranga/external); Pratyahara (5th, bridge); Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi (6th–8th = Antaranga/internal).
Some traditions include Pratyahara in Antaranga; others treat it as the transition between outer and inner yoga.
Niyama (observances) is the 2nd limb (Bahiranga); Pranayama (breath control) is the 4th limb (Bahiranga).
'Dharna' in the option is a variant spelling of Dharana (one-pointed concentration).
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Antaranga sadhana = inner limbs = Dharana/Dhyana/Samadhi (6th-8th); option D (Dharna/Dharana).
Bahiranga = first four (Yama to Pranayama); Antaranga = last three (Dharana to Samadhi).

sources.title: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali — Ashtanga Yoga eight limbs

MPPSC-2024-071.correct_reasoning: Matching rivers to their area of origin: Kaveri rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills (ii); Sabarmati rises in the Mewad hills (iii); Tapti (Tapi) rises in the Satpura range (i); Damodar rises on the Chota Nagpur Plateau (iv). So the code is (1)-(ii), (2)-(iii), (3)-(i), (4)-(iv) = option C. Hence option C is correct.
key_concepts: Kaveri — Brahmagiri hills, Kodagu (Karnataka); called Dakshina Ganga.
Sabarmati — Aravalli/Mewad hills, Rajasthan; flows through Ahmedabad.
Tapti — Satpura range (Betul, MP); one of the few west-flowing peninsular rivers.
Damodar — Chota Nagpur Plateau (Jharkhand/West Bengal); known as the 'Sorrow of Bengal'.
Matching river-origin questions test peninsular drainage knowledge.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Kaveri-Brahmagiri(ii), Sabarmati-Mewad(iii), Tapti-Satpura(i), Damodar-Chota Nagpur(iv) ➜ code C.
West-flowing peninsular rivers: Narmada and Tapti.

sources.title: Indian rivers and their origin — peninsular drainage

MPPSC-2024-072.correct_reasoning: Jharkhand and Odisha together account for more than half of India's total coal reserves (Jharkhand is the largest at ~26% and Odisha second at ~25%; combined ≈ 51–52% under the standard Geological Survey/Ministry of Coal figures). These are options (i) Jharkhand and (iii) Odisha, giving code B. Option C (Odisha and Chhattisgarh ≈ 25% + 17% ≈ 42%) does not exceed 50%. Hence option B is correct. Note: reserve shares vary slightly by source/year, but Jharkhand + Odisha is the standard accepted pair crossing 50%.

option_explanations.reason: Jharkhand qualifies, but Madhya Pradesh holds only about 8% of reserves, so this pair falls short.
Correct. Jharkhand (about 26%) and Odisha (about 25%) together hold slightly over half of India’s coal reserves.
Chhattisgarh and Odisha together hold roughly 43%, short of half.
MP and Odisha together hold only about a third.

key_concepts: Coal reserves by state (approx.): Jharkhand ~26%, Odisha ~25%, Chhattisgarh ~17–18%, West Bengal ~11%, MP ~8%.
Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh form India's 'coal belt' and together hold ~70% of reserves — but no two-state pair other than Jharkhand+Odisha crosses 50% under standard figures.
Jharia (Jharkhand) is the oldest and richest coalfield; Talcher (Odisha) and Ib Valley are major Odisha fields.
Data source matters: GSI/Ministry of Coal figures are the benchmark for this question.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: >50% of India's coal ➜ Jharkhand + Odisha (the top two reserve-holding states).
Chhattisgarh is third (~17%), so Odisha+Chhattisgarh (~42%) does not cross 50%.

sources.title: State-wise coal reserves of India — Geological Survey of India / Ministry of Coal

MPPSC-2024-072.note: The bank's earlier key (C) was corrected to B because Odisha+Chhattisgarh (~42%) does not exceed 50%, whereas Jharkhand+Odisha (~51-52%) does under standard figures. Reserve shares vary slightly by source/year, so this is noted as data-dependent.

MPPSC-2024-074.correct_reasoning: Odisha has the largest deposits of bauxite among Indian states, accounting for about 41% of the country's bauxite resources, followed by Chhattisgarh (~20%) and Andhra Pradesh. Bauxite is the principal ore of aluminium. Hence option B (Odisha) is correct.
key_concepts: Odisha's bauxite is mainly in the Eastern Ghats (Kalahandi, Kandhamal, Rayagada, Sundargarh).
Niyamgiri hills (Odisha) bauxite mining was a notable environmental/forest-rights case (Vedanta).
Jharkhand is known more for coal and iron ore; Gujarat for bauxite in some contexts but not the largest.
India is self-sufficient in bauxite; aluminium plants (e.g., Hirakud, Odisha) use it.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Largest bauxite deposits ➜ Odisha (~41% of India's bauxite).
Odisha = bauxite leader; Chhattisgarh second; Niyamgiri = famous bauxite hills.

sources.title: Mineral resources of India — bauxite by state
sources.citation: Indian Bureau of Mines / NCERT geography

MPPSC-2024-075.correct_reasoning: The statement that is NOT correct is that El Niño occurs every year. El Niño is the periodic warming of the central/eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean that recurs irregularly roughly every 2–7 years (not annually) and typically weakens the Indian monsoon. La Niña (cooling) generally strengthens the Indian monsoon. Hence option C (El Niño occurs every year) is the false statement and is correct for this 'not correct' question.

option_explanations.text: El Nino is an ocean current, which appears off the Peru coast.
El Nino weakens the Indian Monsoon.
La Nina strengthens the Indian Monsoon.

key_concepts: El Niño = warm phase of ENSO (El Niño–Southern Oscillation); appears off Peru/Ecuador around Christmas (hence 'the Christ Child').
During El Niño, the Walker circulation weakens, reducing monsoon rainfall over India (often drought years).
La Niña = cool phase; generally favours a stronger Indian monsoon.
ENSO events are episodic (every few years), not annual — making 'occurs every year' the incorrect statement.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: El Niño ➜ not every year (every 2–7 years); weakens Indian monsoon. La Niña strengthens it.
For 'not correct' questions, pick the false statement: C.

sources.title: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian monsoon — IMD / NCERT geography

MPPSC-2024-076.correct_reasoning: West Bengal has been the largest rice-producing state in India for many years and remained so in 2021–22 (about 14.9–15+ million tonnes), ahead of Uttar Pradesh and Punjab. Hence option D (West Bengal) is correct.
key_concepts: Rice is a kharif crop; West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Andhra Pradesh/Telangana and Tamil Nadu are major producers.
West Bengal leads due to its high yield and multiple crop seasons (aus, aman, boro) in the Gangetic delta.
Punjab is the largest wheat contributor to the central pool, not rice.
This is a standard 'largest producer of crop' fact repeated in prelims.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Largest rice-producing state in India ➜ West Bengal.
Punjab = wheat (central pool); West Bengal = rice.

sources.title: Rice production by state, 2021-22 — Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare

MPPSC-2024-077.correct_reasoning: Among the rivers listed, the Narmada is the longest (about 1,312 km), flowing westwards through Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat to the Arabian Sea. It is the longest river in Madhya Pradesh and the largest west-flowing peninsular river. Hence option C (Narmada) is correct.
key_concepts: Kaveri (~800 km) is longer than Tapti (~724 km) and Son (~784 km) but shorter than Narmada (~1,312 km).
Narmada originates at Amarkantak (MP) and is known as the lifeline of MP; Tapti rises in the Satpura range (Betul, MP).
Son is a tributary of the Ganga, rising near Amarkantak too.
Among MP's rivers, Narmada is the longest; the question's options make Narmada the clear answer.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Longest river among the options ➜ Narmada (~1,312 km), MP's lifeline.
Narmada & Tapti = west-flowing peninsular rivers from MP.

sources.title: Rivers of Madhya Pradesh — Narmada, Tapti, Son

MPPSC-2024-078.correct_reasoning: Cyclone Tauktae struck the western coast of India in May 2021, making landfall in Gujarat on 17 May 2021 as an extremely severe cyclonic storm — the most powerful storm to hit Gujarat in decades. Hence option B (Tauktae) is correct.
key_concepts: Amphan (2020) hit West Bengal–Odisha (east coast); Fani (2019) hit Odisha; Michaung (2023) hit Andhra Pradesh/Tamil Nadu.
